preamble: Loss of glottalization and affrication: Proto-Semitic emphatic *ṣ, reconstructed as the ejective affricate *tsʼ, ends up as plain [s]. In Akkadian this happens directly but rarely under Geers's law, since ṣ is the most stable emphatic and yields only exceptionally (siāqu 'be narrow', from a root with lateral *ṣ́ that had merged with ṣ); Akkadian s may itself still have been [ts] at the time. More often the endpoint is reached via pharyngealized sˤ (*tsʼ > sˤ > s) in Maltese and Cypriot Maronite Arabic.

examples.from: Pre-Akkadian *ṣ (< Proto-Semitic *ṣ́) in the root ṣ-y-q 'be narrow'
examples.note: Proto-Semitic lateral *ṣ́ had already merged with *ṣ in Akkadian; the sibilant then loses emphasis next to the kept q. Arabic ḍāqa 'be narrow', Hebrew ṣûq 'constrain, press upon'. Described as 'very rare' (Shaffer 2007).
